newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean braves minefields to defect to South.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean braves minefields to defect to South.

text.p: A North Korean soldier braved minefields and wire barriers on Monday to flee his famine-threatened homeland and defect to South Korea.
A South Korean defence ministry spokesman said the soldier, identified only as a 22-year-old sergeant, crossed the four km (2.5 mile) wide demilitarised zone (DMZ) bisecting the Korean peninsula.
The heavily guarded DMZ was created as a buffer zone between the rival states under the 1953 truce that ended the three-year Korean War. The DMZ is riddled with thousands of mines.
"A North Korean sergeant defected to our side by seeking asylum at a guard post in the western sector of the frontier at 9:17 a.m. (0017 GMT)," the spokesman said.
He did not say how the soldier had slipped through the zone sealed off from the public by barbed wire and closely patrolled by communist troops.
The defector, who was wearing a blue athletic uniform and sports shoes, was being questioned by South Korean military officials.
A growing number of North Koreans have defected to South Korea recently. International aid agencies have warned that the food crisis threatening the communist state could become critical this summer.
In February, a North Korean woman fled barefood through the eastern sector of the DMZ, saying she wanted to escape poverty.
Less than two hours after the North Korean sergeant sought asylum at the Cold War frontier, a consignment of food aid left the southern port of Pusan for North Korea.
A Red Cross official said the South Korean vessel Changyong 8, carrying 1,000 tonnes of flour and 100,000 boxes of instant noodles, was due to arrive at the North Korean port of Hungnam on Wednesday.
A South Korean tycoon and Christian groups donated the food in response to a Red Cross appeal to help the communist country avoid famine, he said.
The shipment is part of 50,000 tonnes of food the South Korean Red Cross has promised to deliver by the end of next month.

An official of the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said on Friday more than five million North Koreans were near starvation and could die in the next few months unless food arrived.
Ole Gronning, IFRC's representative in Pyongyang, said that based on U.N. estimates of the coming harvest in October, the food deficit was expected to be worse in 1998 than in 1997.
North Korea, hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996, has appealed for international food aid.
